blocks.text: On a busy ward round a team of six clinicians moves between eight beds in forty minutes. Each person touches skin, bedrails, drips and a shared stethoscope. Healthcare-associated infections are often spread on hands, and cleaning them at the right moments is the single most effective routine measure to stop that spread.

blocks.markdown: **Hand hygiene** is the cleaning of the hands either with **soap and water** (handwashing) or with an **alcohol-based hand rub**. It protects patients from organisms carried on the hands of staff and protects staff from organisms picked up from patients and their surroundings. Good hand hygiene depends on three things: **knowing when** (the indications), **choosing how** (soap and water or alcohol rub), and **using the correct technique**.

blocks.title: The five moments for hand hygiene
blocks.text: The World Health Organization identifies five moments when hand hygiene must be performed: (1) before touching a patient, (2) before a clean or aseptic procedure, (3) after body fluid exposure risk, (4) after touching a patient, and (5) after touching patient surroundings.

blocks.caption: The WHO five moments, with the purpose of each
rows: Protect the patient from organisms on your hands
Before a clean or aseptic procedure
Prevent organisms entering the patient, for example through a cannula site
Protect yourself and the environment from the patient's organisms
Protect yourself and other patients from contaminated surfaces such as bedrails

blocks.title: Identifying the moments in a routine task
blocks.prompt: A student walks to a bed, examines the patient's abdomen, then adjusts the bed table and walks to the next bed. At which points is hand hygiene indicated?

steps.text: On arrival at the bed, before touching the patient: moment 1, so clean the hands.
After examining the abdomen: moment 4, after touching the patient.
Adjusting the bed table touches the patient's surroundings: moment 5. Cleaning the hands once after the contact and the table, before leaving the bed area, covers moments 4 and 5.
Before the next patient, moment 1 applies again; hands cleaned on leaving the previous bed satisfy it provided nothing contaminated has been touched since.

blocks.answer: Clean the hands before touching the patient and after leaving the bed area, which covers the contact (moment 4) and the surroundings (moment 5).

blocks.markdown:
### Soap and water or alcohol rub?

Both methods work, but the situation decides which to use.

- **Alcohol-based hand rub** is the preferred method when the hands are **not visibly soiled**. It is faster, kills most organisms and is gentler on skin when used regularly.
- **Soap and water** must be used when the hands are **visibly dirty or contaminated with blood or body fluids**, after using the toilet, and when caring for patients with **diarrhoeal illnesses such as *Clostridioides difficile* or norovirus**, because alcohol does not reliably destroy spores of *C. difficile*.

blocks.caption: Choosing between alcohol rub and soap and water
rows: Hands look clean; between patients on a ward round
Quick and effective on visibly clean hands
Hands visibly soiled with blood or body fluid
Physical removal of soil is needed
After caring for a patient with C. difficile diarrhoea
Alcohol does not reliably kill spores

blocks.markdown:
### Technique for handwashing with soap and water

Before starting: remove wrist watches and bracelets, roll up sleeves (bare below the elbows) and keep nails short and clean. A full wash takes **40 to 60 seconds**; an alcohol rub takes **20 to 30 seconds** until the hands are dry.

1. Wet the hands under running water.
2. Apply enough soap to cover all surfaces.
3. Rub **palm to palm**.
4. Right palm over the **back of the left hand** and vice versa.
5. Palm to palm with **fingers interlaced**.
6. **Backs of fingers** against opposite palms with fingers interlocked.
7. Rotational rubbing of each **thumb** clasped in the opposite palm.
8. Rotational rubbing of the **fingertips** in the opposite palm.
9. **Rinse** under running water.
10. **Dry** thoroughly with a single-use towel.
11. Use the towel to turn off the tap, then discard it.

blocks.title: Choosing a method
blocks.prompt: A student has just helped a 75-year-old patient who has had profuse watery diarrhoea, and there is stool on the bed linen. What method should the student use to clean the hands, and why?

steps.text: Observe the situation: possible contamination with body fluid and a diarrhoeal illness.
Rule: visible contamination or suspected C. difficile or norovirus requires soap and water.
Reason: physical washing removes soiling and spores, which alcohol does not reliably kill.
Perform the full 40 to 60 second technique, drying with a single-use towel.

blocks.answer: Soap and water for 40 to 60 seconds.

blocks.markdown:
### Measuring compliance

Hospitals audit hand hygiene by observing opportunities (moments when hand hygiene was required) and counting how many were taken. Compliance is expressed as a percentage:

blocks.caption: Observation audit as used in hospital infection control programmes.

blocks.title: Gloves are not a substitute
blocks.text: Gloves do not replace hand hygiene. Clean the hands before putting gloves on and after taking them off, because gloves can have tiny defects and the hands can be contaminated when gloves are removed.

blocks.title: Damaged skin
blocks.text: Cover cuts and abrasions with a waterproof dressing. Skin that is cracked or inflamed cannot be cleaned effectively and may carry more organisms.

points: The five moments are before touching a patient, before a clean or aseptic procedure, after body fluid exposure risk, after touching a patient, and after touching patient surroundings.
Use alcohol rub for visibly clean hands and soap and water for visibly soiled hands, after the toilet, and with C. difficile or norovirus.
A handwash takes 40 to 60 seconds and covers palms, backs, between fingers, thumbs and fingertips, followed by rinsing and drying with a single-use towel.
Compliance is measured as the percentage of observed opportunities in which hand hygiene was performed.

questions.stem: Which is one of the WHO five moments for hand hygiene?

options.text: Before a clean or aseptic procedure
Only at the start of the shift
Only after using a computer
Only when hands are visibly dirty

questions.correctOptionText: Before a clean or aseptic procedure

distractorRationale.b: Hand hygiene is needed at multiple points, not just at the start.
distractorRationale.c: Not one of the five moments.
distractorRationale.d: Hands can be contaminated without visible soiling.

questions.explanation: The five moments are tied to patient contact and procedures, not to the clock. Moment 2 protects the patient from organisms entering through a procedure site.

questions.stem: A student has just removed a dressing from a patient's wound and the gloves she wore are visibly stained. Which moment does hand hygiene afterwards most directly correspond to?

options.text: After body fluid exposure risk
Before touching a patient
Before a clean or aseptic procedure
After touching patient surroundings

distractorRationale.a: Correct: moment 3 applies after any exposure risk to body fluids.
distractorRationale.b: This is about the next contact, not what just happened.
distractorRationale.c: It is about preparing for a procedure.
distractorRationale.d: The contamination came from the patient, not the surroundings.

questions.explanation: Moment 3 covers exposure to body fluids such as wound exudate. Even if gloves were worn, the hands must be cleaned after they are removed.

questions.stem: A student has just examined a 68-year-old man with watery diarrhoea caused by Clostridioides difficile. How should she clean her hands?

options.text: Wash with soap and water
Use alcohol rub only
Wipe with a dry tissue
No cleaning is needed if gloves were worn

distractorRationale.a: Correct: soap and water physically removes spores.
distractorRationale.b: Alcohol does not reliably destroy C. difficile spores.
distractorRationale.c: A dry tissue does not clean the hands.
distractorRationale.d: Gloves do not remove the need for hand hygiene.

questions.explanation: C. difficile forms spores that are resistant to alcohol. Mechanical washing with soap and water is needed to remove them from the skin.

questions.stem: Which step of the handwashing sequence comes immediately after rinsing?

options.text: Drying with a single-use towel
Applying soap
Rubbing palm to palm
Wetting the hands

questions.explanation: The order is wet, soap, rub all surfaces, rinse, dry. Wet hands spread organisms more readily, so thorough drying is essential.

questions.stem: Which statement about handwashing technique is correct?

options.text: A full wash with soap and water takes about 40 to 60 seconds and includes the thumbs and fingertips
A 5-second rinse under cold water is enough
Only the palms need to be washed
Wrist watches may be worn if they are waterproof

questions.correctOptionText: A full wash with soap and water takes about 40 to 60 seconds and includes the thumbs and fingertips

distractorRationale.a: Correct: whole hands including thumbs and fingertips, taking 40 to 60 seconds.
distractorRationale.c: Backs, between the fingers, thumbs and fingertips are often missed.
distractorRationale.d: Watches and bracelets should be removed because they harbour organisms.

questions.explanation: Thumbs, fingertips and between-finger spaces are the areas most often missed. The recommended duration of 40 to 60 seconds ensures all surfaces are cleaned.

questions.stem: True or false: alcohol-based hand rub is the preferred method when the hands are not visibly soiled.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Alcohol rub is quicker, kills most organisms and is less drying for the skin with regular use. Soap and water is reserved for visible soiling, toilet use and spore-forming organisms.

questions.stem: A student wears gloves to take a blood sample from a 40-year-old woman. After removing the gloves, which is correct?

options.text: Clean the hands, because gloves do not replace hand hygiene and the hands may be contaminated during removal
No cleaning is needed because the gloves protected the hands
Clean the hands only if blood is visible on them
Wipe the hands on the uniform

questions.correctOptionText: Clean the hands, because gloves do not replace hand hygiene and the hands may be contaminated during removal

distractorRationale.a: Correct: hand hygiene is still needed after glove removal.
distractorRationale.b: Gloves can have defects and hands become contaminated on removal.

questions.explanation: Gloves reduce but do not eliminate contamination. After a body fluid exposure risk the hands must be cleaned after glove removal.

questions.stem: During an audit a ward observer records 48 hand hygiene opportunities, and the clinicians performed hand hygiene on 36 of them. What is the compliance, as a percentage?
questions.explanation: Compliance equals actions performed divided by opportunities observed, times 100, which is 36 divided by 48 multiplied by 100 = 75%. Auditing in this way lets wards track and improve practice.

questions.stem: List the five moments for hand hygiene and explain, for any two of them, whom the hand hygiene protects.
markingGuide: Before a clean or aseptic procedure
Before touching a patient and before aseptic procedures protect the patient
After body fluid exposure, after touching a patient and after surroundings protect the staff member and other patients
questions.explanation: The moments are tied to the direction of risk: before-moments protect the patient and after-moments protect staff and the environment. A strong answer links each moment to who is protected.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man on the ward has a wound with visible discharge on his hands after dressing removal. Explain how you would decide whether to use alcohol rub or soap and water, and describe the handwashing technique you would use.
markingGuide: Visible soiling or body fluids means soap and water
Alcohol rub only if hands are visibly clean
Soap and water also for C. difficile, norovirus and after the toilet
Remove watches, bare below the elbows
Wet, soap, palm to palm, backs of hands, interlaced fingers, backs of fingers, thumbs, fingertips
Rinse and dry with a single-use towel
Use the towel to turn off the tap
questions.explanation: The choice of method depends on the state of the hands and the organism concerned. The technique must cover all surfaces and end with thorough drying.
